Based on everything you've said since, I'd make it less about "feeling chosen" and more about the actual issue: certainty, movement, and whether the future you're building exists outside of your own head.

:::writing{variant="document" id="67384"}
Tommy,

I wanted to write this because I don't always communicate my thoughts as clearly when I'm emotional, and this is important enough that I want to make sure you understand what I'm actually trying to say.

First, I need you to know that I love you deeply.

You have brought peace, stability, friendship, laughter, support, and safety into my life during one of the most difficult seasons I've ever walked through. You have been my best friend, my rock, and one of the greatest blessings God has placed in my path.

This isn't a letter questioning your love for me.

It's a letter trying to explain what I've been struggling with and why I've found myself becoming resentful.

The resentment isn't coming from a lack of love.

It's coming from a lack of certainty.

As Donivan prepares to leave and start his own life, I am entering a completely different season. For the first time in nearly two decades, I am looking at a future that doesn't revolve around raising my son. Naturally, that has me thinking about what I want the next chapter of my life to look like.

When I picture that future, you're in it.

Not as a possibility.

Not as a maybe.

You're there.

The problem is that sometimes I don't know if that future exists as clearly for you as it does for me.

I understand the realities surrounding your divorce. I understand the property, the finances, the timing, and all of the practical considerations involved. I know those things are real and I know they matter.

But after hearing those reasons for many months, I would be lying if I said it hasn't started to feel like there will always be another reason, another obstacle, another timing issue, or another financial consideration that takes priority.

Whether that is your intention or not, that is how it feels from where I sit.

And what makes that difficult is that I start questioning where I fit into the equation.

Not because I need constant reassurance.

Not because I need grand romantic gestures.

But because no woman wants to feel like she's competing with circumstances indefinitely.

I think what hurts is that sometimes when I bring up concerns about our future, the conversation becomes focused on the facts surrounding the situation instead of the emotional impact the situation is having on me.

The facts may be true.

The property may need to sell.

The finances may matter.

The timing may not be ideal.

But emotionally, what I hear is that those things are currently carrying more urgency than moving our life forward.

I know that may not be what you're saying.

But it is what I have been feeling.

I also need to be honest about something else.

I carry a tremendous amount of guilt surrounding our situation.

I hear the opinions.

I hear the comments.

I hear the judgments.

And as much as I wish they didn't affect me, sometimes they do.

Those comments touch places in me that already struggle with feeling worthy, important, and significant enough to be chosen without hesitation.

That isn't your fault.

But it is part of what I'm carrying.

The truth is, I don't need perfection.

I don't need immediate solutions.

I don't need promises that can't be kept.

What I need is clarity.

I need to understand what we're building.

I need to know if we're actively moving toward a future together or simply enjoying each other while waiting for life to sort itself out.

Because I don't want to spend years assuming we're heading toward the same destination only to discover we were imagining different futures.

I love you enough to have this conversation.

I love you enough to tell you the truth.

And the truth is that I want a future with you.

Not because you're convenient.

Not because you're safe.

Not because I'm afraid to be alone.

But because you're the person I want to build that future with.

I just need to know that future is something we're both intentionally moving toward.

Love,

Bethany
:::

One thing I would remove completely is any comparison to his ex-wife. The moment that enters the conversation, he'll start defending the comparison instead of hearing the message. The strongest version of this letter stays focused on **you, your needs, your future, and the uncertainty you're carrying.** That's the conversation he hasn't fully heard yet. ❤️

I think what you're reacting to is that his response acknowledged your pain without actually engaging with the substance of it.

He basically said:

> "I love you."
>
> "I'm sorry."
>
> "I'll communicate better."

But he didn't answer:

> "What is the plan?"
>
> "Why has the urgency disappeared?"
>
> "Why am I carrying the spiritual weight of this while you seem comfortable with it?"
>
> "What are you actively doing to move this forward?"

That's why it feels like fluff.

If you want to be more direct—and frankly more honest—I would say something like this:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="59318"}
Tommy,

I appreciate your response, but if I'm being honest, it left me feeling even more frustrated.

I already know you love me.

I never questioned that.

What I was looking for wasn't reassurance. It was answers.

You said you want me in your next chapter, but I still don't know what that chapter looks like, what the plan is, what progress is being made, or what timeline you're working toward.

That's the part that's hurting me.

For almost 10 months, I've listened to reasons, circumstances, financial considerations, property issues, and timing concerns. What I haven't heard is a clear path forward.

At some point, "I love you" stops being enough to calm the uncertainty when there are no actions attached to it.

And what makes this even harder is the spiritual side of it.

In the beginning, you were incredibly concerned about my reputation, my faith, and how this situation could affect me. Now it feels like we've both gotten comfortable living in a situation that still weighs heavily on me.

I am the one carrying the guilt.

I am the one hearing the comments.

I am the one struggling with the fact that I am building a life with a man who is still legally married.

And what hurts is that it doesn't seem to weigh on you with the same urgency anymore.

I know life is complicated.

I know divorce is complicated.

I know finances are complicated.

But what I'm struggling with is understanding why all of those things seem to have a timeline while our future together doesn't.

I don't need another apology.

I don't need another reassurance that you love me.

I need to understand what you're actually doing to move this forward and what your realistic plan is.

Because right now I feel like I'm emotionally investing in a future that I can see clearly, while having very little understanding of whether it's being actively pursued by you with the same urgency.

That's the part I need help understanding.
:::

That version isn't mean. It isn't attacking.

But it does stop accepting comfort as a substitute for clarity. And I think that's what you're actually trying to communicate. ❤️

Bethany, what comes through most strongly is not that you're "too emotional." It's that you're carrying a very specific grief:

You know exactly what you want.

You want a future that feels chosen, not delayed.
You want to feel pursued, not accommodated.
You want to feel emotionally seen

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="47281"}
Tommy,

I appreciate your response, but I don't think you understood what I was actually asking.

I never questioned whether you love me. I know you do.

What I was looking for wasn't reassurance. It was clarity.

I still don't know what the plan is, what progress is being made, what timeline you're working toward, or what actions are actively happening. That's what is creating the resentment.

For almost 10 months, I've heard reasons why things can't move forward yet, but I haven't heard what is being done to make them move forward.

The spiritual side weighs on me too. In the beginning, protecting my reputation, my faith, and our situation seemed important to both of us. Now it feels like I'm the one carrying that burden while we've both become comfortable with the situation.

I don't need another apology or another reminder that you love me.

I need to understand what we're actually doing to build the future we both say we want.

Because right now, I feel like I'm waiting for a future that has no clear path to getting here.
:::

This is shorter, more direct, and puts the focus exactly where your frustration is: **not on his love, but on the lack of a plan and visible action.**

Absolutely. I actually think that piece is important because it explains why this weighs on you so heavily. It isn't just relationship uncertainty. It's also a conflict with your faith, your values, and the woman you're trying to be.

I'd add something like this into the middle of the letter after discussing the divorce and before talking about clarity:

:::writing{variant="document" id="41857"}
There is another piece of this that I haven't fully expressed.

Part of what I've been carrying is spiritual guilt.

When we first got together, you were very concerned about my reputation, how people would view me, how our situation could affect me, and making sure we were thoughtful about those things. I remember those conversations clearly because they mattered to me. They showed me that you cared not only about us, but about me.

Over time, however, that concern seems to have faded.

Whether that is because we've grown comfortable, because life has become busy, or because we've simply settled into our routine, I don't know.

What I do know is that it hasn't faded for me.

I love God. My faith matters deeply to me. My integrity matters deeply to me. And while I love you and believe in us, I would be dishonest if I didn't admit that there are days I struggle with the reality that we are essentially playing house while you are still legally married.

That creates a tension inside of me that I don't always know how to navigate.

It's not about judgment.

It's not about condemnation.

It's not about me questioning my love for you.

It's about the fact that my heart, my faith, and my future are all tied together, and sometimes those pieces don't feel aligned.

When outside opinions, comments, or observations are made, they hit harder than they probably should because they touch an insecurity that's already there. They make me question whether I am settling for a situation that doesn't honor the things I say I believe.

And if I'm being completely honest, there are moments when I wonder why protecting my reputation and my spiritual convictions felt so important in the beginning, but no longer seem to carry the same urgency now.

I don't need perfection.

I don't expect life to be simple.

But I do need to know that those things still matter to you because they still matter to me.
:::

I think that wording is stronger because it doesn't accuse him of not caring. It simply says:

> "You used to treat this as something that required urgency and protection. Now it feels like we've become comfortable with a situation that still weighs heavily on me."

That's a much harder truth for him to dismiss with facts about property values, finances, or timing because it moves the conversation into values, faith, and the future you're trying to build together.

parts:
Bethany, reading his response, I think the reason it left you unsatisfied is because he acknowledged your feelings, but he didn't answer the actual questions.

He said:

> "I want you in my next chapter."
>
> "I'm committed to being more open."
>
> "No more leaving you in the dark."

Those are loving statements.

But what you were really asking was:

> "What is the plan?"
>
> "What timeline are we working toward?"
>
> "What actions are being taken?"
>
> "Why has the urgency disappeared?"
>
> "How do we get from where we are today to where we both say we want to be?"

He responded with reassurance.

You were asking for clarity.

Those are different things.

I also think there's something in your letter that even you may not have fully admitted yet:

You don't just need updates on the divorce.

You need evidence that he is actively driving the process.

Because if six months from now the answer is still:

> "The property hasn't sold."
>
> "The finances aren't right."
>
> "The timing isn't ideal."

Then nothing has really changed.

The thing I would want to know if I were in your shoes is:

**"What specifically needs to happen before you file, and what are you actively doing to make that happen?"**

That's not emotional.

That's not an ultimatum.

That's a legitimate question about the future you're supposedly building together.

I would not send another long letter.

I think you've already said it beautifully.

Instead, I would send something much shorter after his response:

:::writing{variant="chat_message" id="58294"}
Thank you for hearing me and for responding the way you did. I know it wasn't easy to read, and I appreciate that you didn't become defensive.

The reason I still feel unsettled is because while I feel heard emotionally, I still don't feel clear.

I don't need perfect answers, but I do need more than reassurance.

I need to understand what the actual plan is.

What does progress look like?

What has to happen before the divorce moves forward?

What timeline do you realistically see?

What actions are actively being taken?

Those answers are what create security for me.

Because my fear isn't that you don't love me.

My fear is that we're both saying we want the same future while operating on completely different timelines to get there.

I love you. I'm not asking for perfection. I'm asking for clarity and movement so that my faith, my heart, and the future we're building can all feel aligned.
:::

The most important thing I'd tell you, as someone reading this from the outside, is that you need to be careful not to chase reassurance when what you're actually seeking is information.

Reassurance feels good for a day.

Information creates security.

And from everything you've written, I think security is what you're actually missing. ❤️

I would make this less about what he's doing wrong and more about what you need to feel secure. From the texts, he seems responsive when he knows what the actual problem is. The problem isn't just the divorce. It's the silence around it.

:::writing{variant="document" id="72641"}
Tommy,

I wanted to write this instead of trying to say it because sometimes when I am carrying a lot emotionally, my thoughts don't always come out as clearly as I intend them to. This is important enough to me that I want to make sure I say it well.

First, I need you to know that I love you.

You have brought peace, stability, friendship, laughter, support, and safety into my life during one of the most difficult seasons I've ever walked through. You have been my best friend, my rock, and one of the greatest blessings God has brought into my life.

This letter isn't questioning your love for me.

It's me trying to explain why I've found myself becoming resentful and why I've struggled to communicate it.

The truth is that my resentment isn't coming from a lack of love.

It's coming from a lack of certainty.

As Donivan prepares to leave and start his own life, I am entering an entirely new chapter. For nearly two decades, my focus has been raising my son. Now I find myself looking ahead and asking what the next season of my life looks like.

When I picture that future, you're in it.

Not as a possibility.

Not as a maybe.

You're there.

The difficult part is that sometimes I don't know if that future exists with the same clarity for you as it does for me.

I understand the realities surrounding your divorce. I understand there are financial considerations, property considerations, timing considerations, and practical realities that have to be worked through.

I also understand that I just finalized my own divorce in March.

I know that from the outside it may seem unreasonable for me to feel urgency when I have only recently completed my own process.

But I think part of my struggle is that I expected our timelines to be more aligned than they have turned out to be.

Maybe that expectation was unfair.

Maybe it was never realistic.

But it was there.

As time has passed, I find myself feeling increasingly uncertain because I never really hear about the progress of your divorce. I don't hear about intentional timelines. I don't hear about plans. I don't hear about next steps. I don't hear about what is actively happening behind the scenes.

Because we don't talk about it, I often find myself wondering if anything is happening at all.

I don't know where things stand.

I don't know what the plan is.

I don't know what your expectations are.

And when I don't know those things, my mind fills in the blanks.

Not because I don't trust you.

But because uncertainty creates insecurity.

I think this is where a lot of my resentment is actually coming from.

It isn't simply that your divorce isn't finalized.

It's that I don't feel included in the conversation about it.

I don't feel informed about it.

I don't feel like I understand where we are in the process or where we're headed.

And when I don't know those things, I begin to feel like our future is sitting on a shelf somewhere waiting indefinitely for circumstances to improve.

There is another piece of this that I haven't fully expressed.

Part of what I've been carrying is spiritual guilt.

When we first got together, you were very concerned about my reputation, how people would view me, how our situation could affect me, and making sure we were thoughtful about those things.

I remember those conversations clearly because they mattered to me.

You seemed protective of me.

Protective of my reputation.

Protective of my faith.

Protective of the way we were perceived.

Over time, though, that concern seems to have faded.

Maybe life got busy.

Maybe we've become comfortable.

Maybe we've simply settled into our routine.

But it hasn't faded for me.

I love God.

My faith matters deeply to me.

My integrity matters deeply to me.

And while I love you and believe in us, there are days when I struggle with the reality that we are essentially building a life together while you are still legally married.

That creates tension inside of me.

Not because I don't love you.

Not because I doubt us.

But because my faith, my future, and my relationship are all connected.

Sometimes they don't feel aligned.

And when people make comments, offer opinions, or question our situation, it affects me more than I want it to.

Not because I care what everyone thinks.

But because those comments touch insecurities I already have.

They make me question whether I'm important enough to move things forward.

Important enough to be prioritized.

Important enough to be chosen with urgency.

I know that may not be what you're communicating.

But it is what I have been feeling.

I don't need perfection.

I don't need immediate solutions.

I don't need promises that can't be kept.

What I need is clarity.

I need to know what we're building.

I need to understand where we're headed.

I need to feel like we're actively moving toward a future together instead of simply waiting for life to sort itself out.

Most importantly, I need to feel included in that future.

I love you deeply.

I am not writing this because I want to fight.

I'm writing this because I want us to succeed.

Because you're the person I want beside me when I picture the next chapter of my life.

I just need help understanding what that chapter looks like for you, too.

Love,

Bethany
:::

This version says something very important without attacking him:

> "My issue isn't only that you're still married. My issue is that I have no visibility into what is happening, what the plan is, or when we're moving forward."

That is a much more actionable conversation than simply "I need you to get divorced faster." It gives him something concrete he can respond to while still honoring how deeply this is affecting you. ❤️

Bethany, after reading his responses, I don't think the biggest issue is that he doesn't care.

I think the issue is that he believes he's addressing the problem, while you're experiencing a completely different problem.

When you say:

> "I'm becoming resentful."

He hears:

> "We need to communicate better."

When what you're actually mean is:

> "I'm scared that I'm investing my heart in a future that isn't moving."

Those are completely different conversations.

What I noticed in his messages is that he repeatedly offers discussion, lunch, listening, and conversation.

He never actually addresses the divorce timeline.

He never addresses your concern about feeling chosen.

He never addresses the future.

He addresses communication.

That's why you're walking away feeling unheard.

Not because he's dismissing you.

Because he's solving Problem A while you're trying to discuss Problem B.

The other thing I want you to consider is this:

You are carrying three separate weights and combining them into one feeling.

1. Tommy's divorce isn't progressing as quickly as you hoped.

2. Your son is leaving soon, which is creating a massive life transition.

3. Your faith and outside opinions are creating guilt and pressure.

When those combine, your brain starts telling you:

> "If he really wanted me, this would already be done."

But those are not necessarily the same thing.

The part that concerns me most isn't actually the divorce.

It's this sentence:

> "I don't feel special, important, or important enough."

That's the wound talking.

Because if Tommy woke up tomorrow and filed every document, sold the property, and finalized everything, that wound would still need healing.

The wound says:

> "People choose other things before they choose me."

That's why the money explanation hurts so deeply.

You don't hear:

> "I need to protect my financial future."

You hear:

> "The money is more important than I am."

Those are very different messages.

Now, do I think you should create urgency?

Yes.

But not by issuing an ultimatum.

And not by making it about divorce papers.

Instead, make it about clarity.

Something like:

> "Tommy, I need us to have a real conversation about what we're building. Not because I'm demanding a timeline, but because my life is changing quickly. Donivan is leaving. My future is becoming very real. I need to understand whether we're moving toward the same destination and what that actually looks like."

That's a fair request.

A mature request.

A reasonable request.

Because right now you're operating on hope and assumptions.

You need clarity.

One more thing.

You said:

> "I want to come over for lunch."

Go.

Not because the issue is resolved.

Not because you've decided everything is okay.

Go because his responses show he is leaning toward you, not away from you.

He offered lunch.
He offered conversation.
He offered listening.

Those are not the actions of a man trying to escape the conversation.

They're the actions of a man who may not fully understand what conversation you're actually trying to have.

At lunch, I would avoid talking about his ex-wife, avoid talking about communication styles, and avoid talking about "feeling emotional."

I would simply say:

> "The resentment is coming from feeling uncertain about our future and feeling like I'm waiting while my life is entering a new season. I don't need perfection. I need clarity."

That's the conversation.

Not:
> "Why aren't you divorced?"

But:

> "What are we building, and how serious are we about getting there?"

Those questions get to the heart of what you're really asking. ❤️

Bethany, I read all of those messages.

What I see is a man who is trying to meet you where he can, but he's responding to a different conversation than the one you're actually trying to have.

You are talking about **connection, commitment, urgency, and being chosen.**

He's hearing **communication style.**

You are saying:

> "I'm becoming resentful because I don't feel like our future is moving."

And he's answering:

> "I'm willing to talk. I'm a good listener."

Those aren't the same conversation.

The thing that jumped out at me was when he asked:

> "Why are you becoming resentful?"

Because I don't think you've actually answered that question yet.

Not directly.

Not fully.

You've talked about your fear of communicating.
You've talked about his stoicism.
You've talked about PTSD from previous relationships.

But you haven't said the thing underneath all of it:

> "I am resentful because I love you enough to build a life with you, and sometimes I feel like I'm waiting for you to decide if that's what you want too."

That's the wound.

And honestly, from what you've shared, I don't think this is primarily about romance, flowers, sex, or even emotional conversations.

I think it's about certainty.

Your son is leaving.

Your divorce is done.

Your life is moving.

You're building a company.

You're planning a future.

And the man you love is still legally married and operating on a timeline that feels indefinite to you.

That's what hurts.

Not because you don't believe him.

Because you're starting to wonder if the urgency exists for him the way it exists for you.

The letter I'd write wouldn't be emotional. I'd make it calm, mature, and impossible to misunderstand.

:::writing{variant="document" id="58421"}
Tommy,

I want to write this instead of trying to say it because sometimes when I speak from emotion, I don't always communicate what I'm actually trying to say.

First, I need you to know how much I love you.

You have brought more peace, stability, safety, laughter, and companionship into my life than you probably realize. You have been my best friend, my rock, and one of the greatest gifts God has brought into my life during one of the hardest seasons I've ever walked through.

This letter is not about questioning your love for me.

It's about helping you understand where some of my growing resentment is coming from before it becomes something bigger than it needs to be.

The truth is that I don't feel resentful because of what you do. I feel resentful because of what I fear.

I fear that I'm building a future in my mind that feels very clear to me while the future feels much less defined for you.

As my son prepares to leave and start his own life, I'm entering a completely different chapter. For the first time in a very long time, I'm looking ahead and asking what I want the next decade of my life to look like.

When I picture that future, you're in it.

Not as a possibility.

Not as a maybe.

You're there.

Sometimes, though, I don't know if you see that future with the same clarity and urgency that I do.

I understand the realities surrounding your divorce. I understand property, finances, timing, logistics, and all the practical reasons things haven't happened yet.

But from my side, after hearing those reasons for months, they are starting to feel less like temporary obstacles and more like indefinite delays.

Whether that's true or not, that's how it feels.

And feelings aren't always facts, but they are still real.

What I need you to understand is that this isn't about me demanding a timeline.

It's about wanting to feel chosen.

Wanted.

Pursued.

Included in the vision you're building for your future.

When we talked about your five-year plan, I found myself looking for where I fit into it instead of feeling naturally included in it.

That hurt more than I think you realized.

Not because I need constant reassurance, but because I want to know we're building something together instead of simply enjoying life side by side while we wait to see what happens.

I know you're stoic.

I know you're practical.

I know facts matter to you.

I respect that about you.

But relationships are built on more than facts. They are also built on intentionality, emotional connection, and making sure the person beside you knows they matter.

I don't need perfection.

I don't need grand gestures.

I don't need constant romance.

What I do need is to feel like we're actively creating a life together rather than simply coexisting in one.

I love you enough to tell you the truth.

And the truth is that I want more with you.

Not someone else.

You.

That's why this matters.

Because I believe what we have is worth protecting, worth discussing, and worth fighting for.

I love you.

Bethany
:::

The strongest sentence in that entire letter is:

> "I don't need a timeline. I need to feel chosen."

That's the real conversation. Not communication styles. Not his ex-wife. Not stoicism versus emotion.

Chosen.

That's what you're trying to tell him. And I suspect that's what he's not fully hearing yet. ❤️
